title: Cloning
summary: Explains git clone as the way to copy a remote GitHub repository, with its full commit history, into a local working directory. Demonstrates cloning and running two open-source JavaScript projects (a browser Quake port and a Wordle clone) and points to beginner-friendly projects for first open-source contributions.

concepts.heading: What git clone does
points: git clone <url> downloads a remote repository: every file, every commit and the whole version history, into a new folder on your machine.
The result is a complete local repository. You normally clone once, then keep working on your own branches and pull or push afterwards.
It is the reverse of the previous lesson's push: push sends local commits to a remote, clone brings a remote down for the first time.
The URL is the repository's GitHub address (https form ending in .git, copied from the green Code button).

concepts.heading: Why clone someone else's project
points: Customise an open-source program to your own needs.
Extend it with features it lacks.
Self-host free alternatives to paid tools (project management, newsletter, time tracking); curated lists of such self-hosted apps exist on GitHub.
Reading and modifying other people's code is one of the fastest ways to improve as a developer.

concepts.heading: Workflow: clone, install, run
points: Clone the repo in a terminal, then cd into the new folder it created.
Read the repo's README for run instructions; JavaScript projects usually need npm install to fetch dependencies listed in package.json.
Some projects need extra setup commands (the Quake demo needed a content-server setting copied from its README before starting).
Start the app as the README says: node <file> or npm start. The terminal prints the local address (e.g. port 8080 for Quake) to open in the browser.
Because the code is now on your disk you can rename things, change colours, or alter game rules and re-run.

concepts.heading: Examples used
points: QuakeJS: the classic Quake game compiled to run in a browser, served by a small Node server on port 8080. Use the exact URL the README specifies.

Word Mastermind: a Wordle clone in plain JavaScript, HTML and CSS. After npm install and npm start it opens on a local address. The dict folder holds the word lists (including other languages) and the src folder holds the game logic.
The motivation for the clone was to play more than one word per day, which the official game forbids.

concepts.heading: Next step: contributing to open source
points: The awesome-for-beginners repository lists projects that welcome first-time contributors.
Contributing requires branches, merging and pull requests, covered in the following lessons.

code_examples.caption: Clone, install and run a Node-based project
code_examples.code:
git clone https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>.git
cd <repo>
npm install
npm start

task.name: Clone and run an open-source repo
task.starting_point: A terminal with git, Node and npm installed.
task.goal: Clone a public JavaScript project from GitHub and run it locally, then make a small change.
steps: Pick a project such as the Wordle clone or QuakeJS and copy its clone URL from GitHub.
Run git clone with that URL, then cd into the folder.
Follow the README: npm install, then any extra commands, then npm start or node.
Open the printed local address in the browser.
Browse the source and change something small (title, colours, word list).
task.expected_result: The game runs in the browser from your local copy and your small edit shows up.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 27 - Git, Github and Version Control/27.03 - Cloning/Example.txt

pitfalls: Forgetting to cd into the cloned folder before npm install.
Skipping README setup steps, so the app starts but fails to work.
Opening a different URL from the one the README specifies when the app is tied to it.

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'Cloning a repo': blurb on git clone and why copy someone else's code.
Tasks: (1) write the clone command for a given URL, (2) order the steps clone/cd/install/start, (3) spot the missing cd in a broken command list, (4) identify what package.json is for.
Starter idea: a fake terminal where the learner types commands and gets simulated output.
Interactive demo: an animated diagram of remote repo to local folder showing commits being copied.
